for: services/onboarding/model.js FAMILIES (rho = best achievable composite correlation with the TRUE value) and pool.js (item r)
method: Quotes checked verbatim against the abstract by code (build-validity.js). Validity against the true trait is about sqrt(reliability) x construct loading; where a source gives a reliability the sqrt is applied, where no loading is given the loading is not invented. pessimistic = today (the from-memory values).
scenarios_note: pessimistic = `today`; research-central = `central`; optimistic = `optimistic`. Where the checked evidence says today is too high (ml) central is LOWER than today.

self.basis: Ceiling = correlation of an unlimited set of forced-choice self-report items with the true value. Evidence is for self-report against BEHAVIOUR: a questionnaire trait score predicts average behaviour over many occasions at r .42 to .56 (15 experience-sampling studies); single self-evaluations of ability predict performance at mean r .29 (SD .25). Central keeps .45, the bottom of the questionnaire-to-behaviour range; optimistic is the top of it (.56). Single items sit below the questionnaire (Credé 2012 shows very short measures underestimate), so .25 per item is consistent with .29, but no source gives a forced-choice single-item value for these 100 constructs.
self.item_r_note: one forced-choice item r .25 (today). Mabe & West mean r .29 for single self-evaluations of ability against performance (not personality, not forced choice): consistent, not a measurement of these items.

sources.title: The implications of Big Five standing for the distribution of trait manifestation in behavior: Fifteen experience-sampling studies and a meta-analysis.
sources.quote: predicting average levels with correlations between .42 and .56
sources.shows: questionnaire trait standing vs average behaviour over many occasions, r .42 to .56 (the ceiling range used)

sources.title: Validity of self-evaluation of ability: A review and meta-analysis.
sources.quote: mean r = .29
sources.shows: mean validity of self-evaluations of ability against performance, with high variability (SD .25)
sources.abstract_from: fragment of the APA abstract, from a bibliographic mirror (scholar9.com) via WebFetch/WebSearch; full text not seen

sources.title: Why Are Self-Report and Behavioral Measures Weakly Correlated?
sources.quote: Accumulating evidence indicates weak correlations between self-report and behavioral measures of the same construct.
sources.shows: self-report and behaviour correlate weakly, partly because behavioural measures are unreliable

sources.title: An evaluation of the consequences of using short measures of the Big Five personality traits.
sources.quote: particularly the use of single-item measures, can lead researchers to substantially underestimate the role that personality traits play
sources.shows: single-item measures understate trait effects: a longer composite is more valid than one item

self.verdict: partly supported (range .42-.56 against self-reported-trait-to-behaviour is cited; the exact .45 and the per-item .25 are not measured for these items)

goal.basis: The interests-and-goals survey as a reader of motivation measures (identity_alignment, intrinsic_motivation, relevance_demand ...). No source found gives a validity of a stated interest or goal against these constructs.
goal.verdict: unsupported, conservative guess (kept equal in central and optimistic)

wm.basis: Validity against the true trait is about sqrt(reliability) x the task loading on the construct. Reliability evidence: automated Ospan retest .83 and alpha .78; verbal WM span tasks retest .52 to .81. sqrt(.83) = .91 (optimistic ceiling, loading 1); the middle of the retest range, sqrt(.665) = .82 (central). The task loading on the WM construct is not given in any abstract found, so the single 110-second span task at r .65 is below sqrt(reliability) by an amount nobody measured.
wm.item_r_note: span task r .65 today = sqrt(.7 to .83) x an implied loading of about .7 to .8; the loading itself is unsupported

sources.title: An automated version of the operation span task
sources.quote: good internal consistency (alpha = .78) and test-retest reliability (.83)
sources.shows: one automated operation-span task: alpha .78, retest .83

sources.title: The reliability and stability of verbal working memory measures
sources.quote: ranged from .52 to .81
sources.shows: test-retest correlations of seven verbal working-memory span measures over about 6 weeks

sources.title: The Robust Reliability of Neuropsychological Measures: Meta-Analyses of Test–Retest Correlations
sources.quote: ranged from adequate to high (i.e., r=.7 and higher)
sources.shows: meta-analytic neuropsychological test-retest reliabilities; memory and executive scores sometimes lower

wm.verdict: partly supported (reliability is cited, the loading on the construct is not)

speed.basis: Speed-of-processing tasks (symbol matching) have meta-analytic neuropsychological retest reliabilities mostly r .7 and above, so sqrt(.7) = .84 up to sqrt(.8) = .89 is the index ceiling if the task measures the trait with loading 1. Central keeps .80 (a loading below 1); optimistic .89. The SDMT-specific retest figures (oral SDMT .83-.86 in one healthy sample) could not be tied to a verified record in this audit, so they are not counted.
speed.item_r_note: symbol-match r .60 today; loading on a speed construct unsupported (the theory papers cited show speed is a shared factor in cognition but give no loading)

sources.title: The Robust Reliability of Neuropsychological Measures: Meta-Analyses of Test–Retest Correlations
sources.quote: ranged from adequate to high (i.e., r=.7 and higher)
sources.shows: typical meta-analytic retest reliability of widely used neuropsychological scores

sources.title: Symbol Digit Modalities Test: A valid clinical trial endpoint for measuring cognition in multiple sclerosis
sources.quote: the SDMT proved superior to the PASAT
sources.shows: the symbol-digit task was judged the better speed measure in 14 trials of the multiple sclerosis consortium (no coefficient in the abstract)

sources.title: The processing-speed theory of adult age differences in cognition.
sources.quote: considerable shared age-related variance across various measures of speed
sources.shows: speed measures share variance, so one speed task reads a general speed factor

speed.verdict: partly supported (retest reliability supports a high ceiling; the exact .80 and the task loading are not given)

read.basis: Reading rate and comprehension from two short passages. Brysbaert (2019) gives the population mean (238 wpm non-fiction) and says individual differences are reliable, with no coefficient. No source found gives a retest reliability or validity for a 2-passage reading measure.

sources.title: How many words do we read per minute? A review and meta-analysis of reading rate
sources.quote: Within each group/task there are reliable individual differences
sources.shows: reading rate shows reliable individual differences (no coefficient in the abstract); norm 238 wpm for adults

read.verdict: unsupported, conservative guess (kept equal in central and optimistic)

reason.basis: A 9-item reduced Raven form predicts the 60-item total at r .98 in the fitting sample and .90 in held-out data, so a short set of reasoning items can carry most of the full test. The pool has five items of each of five kinds (not nine of one kind), so central keeps .75, below .90; optimistic .85. The correlation with the full-scale SCORE is not validity against the true trait (the full test is itself imperfect), so .90 is not used directly.
reason.item_r_note: one reasoning item r .2 to .35 today; no source gives a single-item value

sources.title: Development of Abbreviated Nine-Item Forms of the Raven’s Standard Progressive Matrices Test
sources.quote: correlations of .9836 and .9782 were achieved for the reduced forms and .9063 and .8978 for the validation data
sources.shows: nine matrix items predict the 60-item total: .98 in fitting data, about .90 in validation data

reason.verdict: partly supported (one source, a lower bound on short-set quality; the pool design differs from the nine-item form)

switch.basis: Task-switching difference scores: reaction-time switch costs were reliable in one well-controlled paradigm (retest ICC .78 and .82; internal consistency .92) but costs from error rates were substantially lower; scoring method changes reliability (Hughes 2014: rate-residual, bin and inverse-efficiency scores beat plain latency cost, no coefficients in the abstract). Other difference-score tasks range from 0 to .82 (Hedge 2018, which tested Flanker, Stroop, stop-signal, go/no-go, Posner, Navon and SNARC, NOT task switching). Today comment "reliability about .5 (Hughes 2014)" is NOT in the abstract: no source states .5. Central keeps .50 (inside the cited 0 to .82 spread, task and scoring dependent); optimistic .71 = sqrt(.5) (loading 1).
switch.item_r_note: one switch block r .30 to .35 today; unsupported as a per-block value

sources.title: Internal consistency and test–retest reliability of an affective task-switching paradigm.
sources.quote: good test-retest reliabilities (ICC(2,1) of .78 and .82, respectively) for response time-based switch costs
sources.shows: RT switch costs in an affective task-switching paradigm: retest ICC .78 and .82; error-rate costs lower

sources.title: Alternatives to switch-cost scoring in the task-switching paradigm: Their reliability and increased validity
sources.quote: the strongest methods were the rate residual and bin score methods
sources.shows: switch-cost scoring changes reliability and validity; alternatives to latency costs beat plain latency scoring

sources.title: The reliability paradox: Why robust cognitive tasks do not produce reliable individual differences
sources.quote: Reliabilities ranged from 0 to .82, being surprisingly low for most tasks given their common use.
sources.shows: seven classic difference-score tasks (not task switching): low reliability from low between-person variance

switch.verdict: partly supported (the range is cited; the figure .5 attributed to Hughes 2014 is not in its abstract)

ml.basis: Chosen behaviour in a short controlled episode is a few occasions, not the many occasions averaged in experience sampling. In 15 experience-sampling studies, trait standing predicted AVERAGE behaviour at r .42 to .56. Single occasions predict far less, so .55 (top of that range) is generous for three choice points. Central .42 (bottom of the range) is itself an upper bound for a short lesson; optimistic .56. The criterion in those studies was self-reported trait standing, not a true value.
ml.item_r_note: one choice point r .15 to .3 today: unsupported; aggregation raises validity with occasions (Epstein 1979 is cited for this in the footprint file but only its title could be checked)

sources.title: The implications of Big Five standing for the distribution of trait manifestation in behavior: Fifteen experience-sampling studies and a meta-analysis.
sources.quote: predicting average levels with correlations between .42 and .56
sources.shows: trait standing against behaviour averaged over many experience-sampling reports

ml.verdict: partly supported (one source; applies to many occasions, so central is lowered below the old .55)

taste.basis: A/B teaching-style taste plus recall of both versions. A review for the learning-styles literature found no adequate evidence that matching instruction to a stated preference improves learning, so preference is not shown to read learning benefit; whether a preference reads the TRAIT (for example inductive_trajectory) is a different question that no source found answers.

sources.title: Learning Styles
sources.quote: Proponents of learning-style assessment contend that optimal instruction requires diagnosing individuals' learning style and tailoring instruction accordingly.
sources.shows: describes the meshing claim the review then tests (its verdict, in the full abstract, is that evidence is lacking)

taste.verdict: unsupported, conservative guess (kept equal in central and optimistic)

conf.basis: Confidence ratings on reasoning items read calibration, self-monitoring and self-efficacy. There is a stable individual-difference confidence factor that goes across test types (Pallier 2002), which supports a trait, but no abstract found gives its reliability, so the "about .5 to .7 over 20+ items" comment is unsupported here.

sources.title: The Role of Individual Differences in the Accuracy of Confidence Judgments
sources.quote: Results again indicated the presence of a confidence factor that transcended the nature of the testing vehicle.
sources.shows: a general confidence factor exists across cognitive and perceptual tests

conf.verdict: unsupported (trait supported; the coefficient is a conservative guess)

truth_correlation.parent_assumption: scripts/scorecard-recovery-sim.js drawTruth: z_j = lg*g + lc*c(category) + specific; cognitive categories (intake, reasoning, transfer) lg .5, lc .3; all others lg .25, lc .4. Implied correlations: cognitive within category .34, cognitive across categories .25, other within .22, other across .06, cognitive-to-other .125.

central.note: average first-factor variance 45.9% (SD 12.9%) in 97 non-Western samples gives an average test loading of about .68 and an average between-test r of about .46; observed tests carry error, so true-score correlations are at least that

high.note: loading from one SD above the 45.9% mean (58.8% of variance)

sources.title: Spearman’s g found in 31 non-Western nations: Strong evidence that g is a universal phenomenon.
sources.quote: The first factor in the initial EFA explained an average of 45.9% of observed variable variance (SD = 12.9%)
sources.shows: a general factor explains about 46% of the variance of cognitive tests (SD 13%)

sources.title: The neuroscience of human intelligence differences
sources.quote: Quantitative genetic studies have established that there are additive genetic contributions to different aspects of cognitive ability--especially general intelligence
sources.shows: general cognitive ability is a replicated construct (no correlation size in the abstract; not used for the number)

cognitive.verdict: parent assumption is too WEAK for the cognitive measures (cross-category r .25 against about .46 observed between tests); central .65 is derived from one meta-analytic figure and applies to ability TESTS, while Savant measures such as intake_baseline are scorecard constructs, so the transfer is an assumption

central.note: unsupported by any verified number: kept

high.note: unsupported guess for a sensitivity run, not a cited value

sources.title: Higher-order factors of the Big Five.
sources.quote: Two higher-order factors were clearly evident in all studies.
sources.shows: the Big Five correlate: two higher-order factors in 14 studies (no correlation sizes in the abstract)

sources.title: The General Factor of Personality: A meta-analysis of Big Five intercorrelations and a criterion-related validity study
sources.quote: two meta-factors Stability and Plasticity
sources.shows: a meta-analysis of Big Five intercorrelations supports two meta-factors and a general factor (no sizes in the abstract fragment)
sources.abstract_from: fragment of the abstract, from a search result (pure.uj.ac.za record); no correlation sizes in it

non_cognitive.verdict: non-zero correlation among personality-like measures is supported (Big Five are not independent); the SIZE could not be checked in any abstract, so .06 across and .22 within are conservative guesses, labelled unsupported
